name: HBM (high-bandwidth memory)
thesis: The memory that makes an accelerator usable — stacked DRAM bonded beside the GPU. Bandwidth, not compute, is the binding constraint, and supply is sold out across all three makers through 2026.

gauge.rationale: Eased slightly as Samsung qualifies HBM4 into Nvidia and all three suppliers ramp — but 2026 supply is sold out across the board and orders are booked into 2028.

why_it_gates: HBM is the stacked DRAM bonded next to the GPU die — bandwidth, not raw compute, is what limits large-model training and inference. Every accelerator needs multiple stacks, and supply is set by just three manufacturers, two of which control ~90% of output. So memory allocation gates how many usable AI chips actually exist, in lockstep with CoWoS packaging downstream.

watchlist.name: SK Hynix
watchlist.role: HBM leader (~62%); ~70% of Nvidia Rubin HBM4

watchlist.name: Samsung Electronics
watchlist.role: First to ship HBM4; entering Nvidia supply

watchlist.name: TSMC
watchlist.role: HBM4 base-die (logic) partner to SK Hynix

catalysts.text: Samsung begins HBM4 mass production; first shipments after Lunar New Year
Nvidia Vera Rubin ramps on HBM4; 16-Hi stacks target Q4 2026
Shortage expected to ease as new fabs (e.g. SK Hynix M15X) land capacity

what_loosens_it: Unlike CoWoS's single source, three suppliers are all ramping hard — Samsung and Micron qualifying HBM4 into Nvidia broadens supply, and TrendForce flags a possible 2026 demand correction from AI-chip delays and inventory. Structurally, though, memory stays sold out through 2026 and most expect real relief only around 2028.

developments.text: Nvidia HBM4 allocation splits ~SK Hynix mid-50%, Samsung mid-20%, Micron ~20%
TrendForce flags converging supply-demand and a 2026 correction phase as HBM4 ramps
All three suppliers sold out through 2026; HBM TAM seen reaching ~$100B by 2028
